claim: Rod-shaped bacterial cells can readily adapt their lengths and widths in response to environmental changes.
source: Rod-shaped bacterial cells can readily adapt their lengths and widths in response to environmental changes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general observation about bacterial behavior.

claim: During steady-state growth, γ = 6.24 ± 0.04 for E. coli.
source: Specifically, during steady-state growth (Si et al., 2017), γ = 6.24 ± 0.04
evidence: This is a specific numerical result obtained from fitting experimental data from Si et al. (2017).

claim: The coefficient of variation for E. coli aspect ratio is approximately 14%.
source: with a coefficient of variation ∼14% (Figure 1B)
evidence: This is a statistical measure calculated from the aspect ratio distribution shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Both cell length and width increase with growth rate when rod-shaped bacteria grow in media with different nutrient availability.
source: When rod-shaped bacteria grow in media with different nutrient availability, both cell length and width increase with growth rate (Schaechter et al., 1958; Si et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited experimental studies.

claim: Control of cell volume in many rod-shaped cells is achieved via an adder mechanism, whereby cells elongate by a fixed length per division cycle.
source: At the single-cell level, control of cell volume in many rod-shaped cells is achieved via an adder mechanism, whereby cells elongate by a fixed length per division cycle (Amir, 2014; Campos et al., 2014; Taheri-Araghi et al., 2015; Deforet et al., 2015; Wallden et al., 2016; Banerjee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies demonstrating the adder mechanism.

claim: The determination of cell size has been linked to a condition-dependent regulation of cell surface-to-volume ratio.
source: A recent study has linked the determination of cell size to a condition-dependent regulation of cell surface-to-volume ratio (Harris and Theriot, 2016).
evidence: This is based on a cited study by Harris and Theriot (2016).

claim: At low nutrient concentrations, cells increase their surface-to-volume ratio to promote nutrient influx.
source: In Equation (1) underlies an adaptive feedback response of the cell — at low nutrient concentrations, cells increase their surface-to-volume ratio to promote nutrient influx (Si et al., 2017; Harris and Theriot, 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mathematical relationship supported by cited studies.

claim: Cell width and length under changes in growth media can be directly predicted from knowing cell volume as a function of cell cycle parameters.
source: Thus, knowing cell volume as a function of cell cycle parameters (Si et al., 2017) we can directly predict cell width and length under changes in growth media, in agreement with experimental data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing model predictions with experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Long Spirochetes deviate from the S≈2πV^(2/3) curve.
source: while the long Spirochetes deviate from this curve (Figure 1D–E)
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Coccoid S. aureus maintains an aspect ratio η = 1.38 ± 0.18 when exposed to different antibiotics.
source: but maintains a much lower aspect ratio η = 1.38 ± 0.18 (Quach et al., 2016) when exposed to different antibiotics
evidence: This is calculated from data in the cited study by Quach et al. (2016).

claim: Aspect-ratio preservation likely emerges from a mechanism that is common to diverse rod-shaped and coccoid bacterial species.
source: Therefore, aspect-ratio preservation likely emerges from a mechanism that is common to diverse rod-shaped and coccoid bacterial species.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both rod-shaped and coccoid bacteria maintain constant aspect ratios.

claim: A fixed aspect ratio is maintained on average for newborn cells across different growth media.
source: suggesting that a fixed aspect ratio is maintained on average
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that S=2πV^(2/3) holds across different media.

claim: Slight deviation from the 2/3 scaling in single-cell data is a consequence of large fluctuations in newborn cell lengths for a given cell width.
source: In the single-cell data, slight deviation from the 2/3 scaling is a consequence of large fluctuations in newborn cell lengths for a given cell width (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is explained by analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: The probability distribution of aspect ratio is independent of the growth media.
source: Importantly, the probability distribution of aspect ratio is independent of the growth media (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the overlapping distributions shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Cellular aspect ratio is independent of cell size as well as growth rate.
source: implying that cellular aspect ratio is independent of cell size as well as growth rate
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that aspect ratio distributions are independent of growth media.

claim: Cell division is triggered when a constant length is added per division cycle.
source: Cell division is triggered when a constant length is added per division cycle — a mechanism that is captured by a model for threshold accumulation of division initiator proteins, produced at a rate proportional to cell size (Basan et al., 2015; Deforet et al., 2015; Ghusinga et al., 2016).
evidence: This is the adder mechanism supported by cited studies.

claim: FtsZ has been identified as the key initiator protein that assembles a ring-like structure in the mid-cell region to trigger septation.
source: a recent study (Si et al., 2019) has identified FtsZ as the key initiator protein that assembles a ring-like structure in the mid-cell region to trigger septation.
evidence: This is based on a cited study by Si et al. (2019).

claim: The total FtsZ scales with the cell width.
source: This is consistent with experimental findings that the total FtsZ scales with the cell width (Shi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental study.

claim: The concentration of FtsZ in an average E. coli cell is in the range 4–10 μM, much higher than the critical concentration 1 μM.
source: It is reasonable to assume that all the FtsZ proteins are in filamentous form at cell division, as the concentration of FtsZ in an average E. coli cell is in the range 4–10 μM, much higher than the critical concentration 1 μM (Erickson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on cited measurements of FtsZ concentration.

claim: Aspect ratio homeostasis is achieved via a balance between the rates of cell elongation and division protein production.
source: Aspect ratio homeostasis is thus achieved via a balance between the rates of cell elongation and division protein production, consistent with observations that FtsZ overexpression leads to minicells and FtsZ depletion induces elongated phenotypes (Potluri et al., 2012; Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the model and supported by cited experimental observations.

claim: Added length correlates with cell width during one cell cycle.
source: Furthermore, added length correlates with cell width during one cell cycle implying that the cell width is a good predictor for added cell length (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is shown by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: After nutrient shift, aspect ratio reaches its pre-stimulus homeostatic value over multiple generations.
source: After nutrient shift, aspect ratio reaches its pre-stimulus homeostatic value over multiple generations.
evidence: This is observed in the model simulations shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Cell shape parameters reach a steady state faster in media with higher growth rate.
source: such that the cell shape parameters reach a steady state faster in media with higher growth rate. This result is consistent with the experimental observation that newborn aspect ratio reaches equilibrium faster in fast growing media (Taheri-Araghi et al., 2015) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is consistent with experimental observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: MreB depletion increases the cell width and slightly decreases cell length while keeping growth rate constant.
source: Second, MreB depletion increases the cell width and slightly decreases cell length while keeping growth rate constant (Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from Zheng et al. (2016).

claim: Cells treated with MreB inhibitor A22 induce envelope stress response system (Rcs) that in turn activates FtsZ overproduction.
source: Furthermore, cells treated with MreB inhibitor A22 induce envelope stress response system (Rcs) that in turn activates FtsZ overproduction (Carballès et al., 1999; Cho et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on cited studies.

claim: Transient long filamentous cells result from exposure to high dosages of cell-wall targeting antibiotics that prevent cell division.
source: Third, transient long filamentous cells result from exposure to high dosages of cell-wall targeting antibiotics that prevent cell division, or DNA-targeting antibiotics that induce filamentation via SOS response (Nonejuie et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from Nonejuie et al. (2013).

claim: Cell-wall targeting antibiotics inhibit the activity of essential septum forming penicillin binding proteins, preventing cell septation.
source: Cell-wall targeting antibiotics inhibit the activity of essential septum forming penicillin binding proteins, preventing cell septation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of cell-wall targeting antibiotics.

claim: For DNA targeting antibiotics, FtsZ is directly sequestered during SOS response resulting in delayed ring formation and septation.
source: For DNA targeting antibiotics, FtsZ is directly sequestered during SOS response resulting in delayed ring formation and septation (Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on a cited study.

claim: Cell width is an essential shape parameter for determining cell length in E. coli.
source: Our study suggests that cell width is an essential shape parameter for determining cell length in E. coli (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: In B. subtilis, cell width stays approximately constant across different media, while elongating in length.
source: This is to be contrasted with B. subtilis, where cell width stays approximately constant across different media, while elongating in length (Sharpe et al., 1998).
evidence: This is based on a cited study.

claim: FtsZ recruitment in B. subtilis is additionally controlled by effector UgtP, which localises to the division site in a nutrient-dependent manner and prevents Z-ring assembly.
source: However, FtsZ recruitment in B. subtilis is additionally controlled by effector UgtP, which localises to the division site in a nutrient-dependent manner and prevents Z-ring assembly (Weart et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on a cited study.

claim: Increasing cell surface-to-volume ratio under low nutrient conditions can result in an increased nutrient influx to promote cell growth.
source: For instance, increasing cell surface-to-volume ratio under low nutrient conditions can result in an increased nutrient influx to promote cell growth (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a proposed adaptive benefit supported by the relationship shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Under translation inhibition by ribosome-targeting antibiotics, bacterial cells increase their volume while preserving aspect ratio.
source: Under translation inhibition by ribosome-targeting antibiotics, bacterial cells increase their volume while preserving aspect ratio (Harris and Theriot, 2016; Si et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on cited experimental observations.

claim: Increasing volume while preserving aspect ratio leads to a reduction in surface-to-volume ratio to counter further antibiotic influx.
source: This leads to a reduction in surface-to-volume ratio to counter further antibiotic influx.
evidence: This is a proposed adaptive benefit inferred from the geometric relationship.

claim: The efficiency of swarming bacteria strongly depends on their aspect ratio.
source: Furthermore, recent studies have shown that the efficiency of swarming bacteria strongly depends on their aspect ratio (Ilkanaiv et al., 2017; Jeckel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on cited studies.

claim: The highest foraging speed has been observed for aspect ratios in the range 4–6.
source: The highest foraging speed has been observed for aspect ratios in the range 4–6 (Ilkanaiv et al., 2017)
evidence: This is based on a cited study.

claim: The maintenance of an optimal aspect ratio may have evolutionary benefits for cell swarmers.
source: suggesting that the maintenance of an optimal aspect ratio may have evolutionary benefits for cell swarmers.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation about foraging speed.

claim: The mechanistic origin of aspect ratio control has been puzzling for almost half a century.
source: whose mechanistic origin has been puzzling for almost half a century (Zaritsky, 1975; Zaritsky, 2015)
evidence: This is stated with reference to historical citations.

claim: The power law exponent for steady-state data is 0.671 ± 0.006.
source: Best fit shown in dashed black line for steady-state data from Si et al. (2017) gives γ = 6.24 ± 0.04, and a power law exponent 0.671 ± 0.006.
evidence: This is obtained from fitting experimental data.
